 Quinn Shephard’s new Netflix drama uses millennial nostalgia to eerie ends.
 Listen · 5:44 min Share full article 
 Kristina Bogic, left, and Sara Boustany lead a dance team with dark secrets in “The Body.” Credit... Netflix By Caroline Darya Framke 
 Caroline Darya Framke is a TV critic at The New York Times. She did not participate in “light as a feather, stiff as a board” sleepover culture, but she does respect it.
 Nov. 13, 2026 The Body

 TV shows may only have a few minutes to snag restless viewers before they click over to something else. It’s why so many series start at the climax before flashing back to reveal how everything unfolded. Better to grab people right away with a blunt twist than lose them to a slow burn.
 The classic move, as procedurals like “Law and Order” have demonstrated for decades, is to open with an untimely death. In that respect “The Body,” now streaming on Netflix, shows some restraint. Instead of starting with the murder implied by the title, the new drama makes the bold choice to tell its story in chronological order.
 The Body 
 Save to your watch list :
 Want to watch Have seen To hook its audience, then, the creator Quinn Shephard offers another form of temptation: languorous shots of Catholic schoolgirls helping each other stretch, eyeing each other hungrily while sinking into the splits. In their matching pink sweatsuits — did I mention that “The Body” takes place in the early 2000s? — they might as well be filming a commercial for Juicy Couture.
 Leaning on such a basic type of sex appeal can be a cynical gambit. But if you stick with “The Body” past its initial clichés, it is clear that Shephard, who also directed the first episode, is purposefully remixing the hypersexualized references of her millennial youth. The show’s visual language includes nods to “The Craft,” “Jennifer’s Body” and “Mean Girls.” These schoolgirls are growing up in a world formed by t.A.T.u.’s “ All the Things She Said ” and Britney Spears’s “ … Baby, One More Time .” They know what people assume about them, and are more inclined to embrace those perceptions than to examine their implications.
 The first of eight episodes kicks off with the high school dance team holding emergency tryouts after a key member breaks her ankle. Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), fresh out of home-school, is desperate to join the team’s built-in circle of glamorous friends. Instead, they choose Grace (Sofia Wylie), whose undeniable dance skills outweigh her inconvenient piety and familial connection to Father Franklin (Nnamdi Asomugha), the school’s head priest and principal. The co-captains, Anya (Kristina Bogic) and Elise (Sara Boustany), turn the team’s Halloween party into an initiation ritual in which they jokingly — or maybe not? — summon Satan.
